options.why: A long-standing quirk from the first JavaScript engine; it can never be fixed without breaking the web.
There is no "null" result from typeof, even though null is its own primitive type.
That is what typeof returns for undefined, not for null.
null coerces to 0 in arithmetic, but typeof does not report it as a number.

explanation: `typeof null === "object"` is a historical bug kept for compatibility. To test for null, compare directly: `value === null`.

options.why: NaN is the only JavaScript value that is not equal to itself, even with strict equality.
Correct: by the IEEE 754 rules NaN compares unequal to everything, including itself.

explanation: Use `Number.isNaN(x)` or `Object.is(x, NaN)` to test for NaN. The global `isNaN()` coerces its argument first, so `isNaN('hello')` is also true.

stem: Complete the call so it returns `true`: `Object.____(NaN, NaN)`. Type just the missing method name.
explanation: `Object.is` implements SameValue equality: it treats `NaN` as equal to `NaN` and distinguishes `+0` from `-0`, unlike `===`.

stem: Which of these values are falsy in JavaScript? (Choose three.)

options.why: Zero (and -0) are falsy numbers.
The empty string is the only falsy string.
null is falsy, as are undefined, NaN, false and 0n.
Any non-empty string is truthy, including the text "false".
All objects are truthy, including empty arrays.
All objects are truthy, however empty they are.

explanation: The falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else, including every object and array, is truthy.

stem: Which of these expressions evaluates to `true`?

options.why: Loose equality treats null and undefined as equal to each other and to nothing else.
null is only loosely equal to undefined; it is not converted to 0 by ==.
NaN is unequal to itself under both == and ===.
Strict equality never converts types, so a string and a number are never ===.

explanation: `null == undefined` is true by a special rule of loose equality. It is why `value == null` is a common shorthand for checking "null or undefined"; prefer `===` everywhere else.

stem: Which array method returns a new array containing the result of calling a function on every element?

options.why: forEach runs the function for side effects and always returns undefined.
map builds a new array of the same length from each callback's return value.
filter returns only the elements whose callback returned a truthy value.
reduce folds the array into a single accumulated value.

explanation: `map` transforms every element and returns a new array, leaving the original untouched.

stem: Match each array method with what it returns.

options.text: The first matching element, or undefined
A new array of every matching element
true if at least one element matches
The index of the first match, or -1

explanation: `find` and `findIndex` stop at the first match, `filter` collects every match, and `some` answers yes or no. No built-in array method counts matches directly; use `filter(...).length` or `reduce`.

length is always a number on an array.

explanation: Objects and arrays are assigned by reference. To copy an array, use `[...a]`, `a.slice()` or `structuredClone(a)`.

stem: `Object.freeze(obj)` also freezes the objects nested inside `obj`.

options.why: freeze is shallow: nested objects stay mutable unless you freeze them too.
Correct: only the top-level properties are frozen.

explanation: `Object.freeze` is shallow. For deep immutability, freeze recursively (or use an immutable data library).

stem: You need a faithful deep copy of an object that contains nested plain objects and a `Date`. Which approaches produce one? (Choose two.)

options.why: The structured clone algorithm copies nested objects deeply and keeps Date objects as Dates.
Spread copies only the top level; nested objects are still shared.
Like spread, Object.assign is a shallow copy.
It is deep, but the Date comes back as a string, and undefined values and functions are dropped.

options.text: A recursive copy function that handles `Date` and plain objects
options.why: A hand-written deep clone works when it explicitly handles every type the object contains.

explanation: Prefer `structuredClone` for deep copies: it handles nesting, Dates, Maps, Sets and cycles. The JSON round-trip silently changes types.
